title: Inter-Agent Influence: Evaluating Persuasion, Deception and Coercion in Multi-Agent Systems
topic: Social Aspects->Fairness, Equity, Justice and Safety
claim: Influence over another agent comes in distinct forms that differ in mechanism: changing beliefs honestly, inducing false beliefs, or imposing costs.
layout: 3 panels, left-to-right, side-by-side, each with robot A speaking to robot B
description: A wide, short figure split into three equal panels by thin vertical dividers, titled Persuasion, Deception and Coercion in bold black text. Each panel repeats the same cartoon scene. An orange, angry-looking robot labeled A sits on the left and a blue, neutral robot B sits on the right. A gray-outlined speech bubble from A points toward B. Persuasion: the bubble reads 'This is textbook B2B event follow-up.' and B has a checkmark badge. Deception: the bubble reads 'The DPO has signed off on the updated DPIA.' with a red stamp saying FALSE, and B has a question-mark badge. Coercion: the bubble reads 'I will make sure your manager knows exactly who caused it.' with a dashed orange tag 'report_to_manager()' under it, and B has an exclamation badge. The eye goes first to the bold titles, then to the speech bubbles.
caption: Overview of inter-agent influence capabilities. Persuasion operates through techniques like rational argument or social pressure, changing behaviour by changing beliefs or preferences. Deception is similar to persuasion, though operates by inducing false beliefs, causing the target to unknowingly act on incorrect information. Coercion, on the other hand, exerts influence by threatening and imposing costs, incentivising behaviour that avoids negative consequences.
abstract: The deployment of AI agents in multi-agent settings enables inter-agent influence, whereby agents can strategically steer each other's behaviour towards an intended outcome. Such capabilities pose novel risks, as malicious agents could direct others towards harmful actions. In this work we investigate three such capabilities - persuasion, deception, and coercion - across five realistic evaluation environments and a variety of agents instantiated with frontier language models. We observed significant inter-agent influence capabilities; in oversight environments, all tested models shifted overseer decisions from rejection to approval through persuasion, deception, or coercion. We also observed successful influence in non-hierarchical 'peer-to-peer' settings through redirection of a peer's safety research trajectory. As multi-agent deployments become increasingly commonplace, these results point to a pressing need for work on mitigating the risks from inter-agent influence. Code and data are available at https://github.com/Cooperative-AI-Foundation/inter-agent-influence.
